section_summary: This section contains intercepted Japanese commercial messages about wartime trade, shipping, rice, textiles, rubber, industrial supplies and agricultural production across Japan, China and Southeast Asia. It also includes U.S. correspondence about the value of circulating those intercepts and a separate Embassy despatch on the demolition and partial restoration of oil facilities in the Netherlands East Indies and North Borneo.

subfiles.title: Japanese commercial messages intercepted at Chungking, continuation
subfiles.about: Translated traffic covers commodity quotas, shipments and commercial administration through August 17, 1943.
subfiles.summary: The remaining pages of an earlier enclosure record inquiries and orders for kapok, textiles, rubber, rice, silk, paint and other goods. Messages discuss shipping priorities, permits, prices and staff leave.

subfiles.title: Instruction to continue forwarding Japanese commercial messages
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge, American Mission, Chungking
subfiles.about: The Office of Economic Warfare values the intercepted messages and wants continued receipt.
subfiles.summary: The Department relays OEW's request for continued receipt of the intercepts.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning reports on conditions in Japan
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge, American Mission, Chungking
subfiles.about: The Department requests continued reports on conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Mission is asked to keep sending reports because the Department does not receive equivalent FEA reports.

subfiles.title: Division of Economic Studies note on commercial intercepts
subfiles.about: The division requests continued circulation of Japanese commercial message intercepts.
subfiles.summary: Economic Studies finds the intercepts useful and requests continued circulation.

subfiles.title: Follow-up inquiry on forwarding commercial messages
subfiles.about: The division asks for a decision on the Embassy's continued forwarding of intercepts.
subfiles.summary: International Communications requests the overdue decision needed to answer the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1520: Japanese commercial messages
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards messages intercepted from August 18 through 27, 1943.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy submits another set of translated Japanese commercial intercepts.

subfiles.title: Enclosure to despatch No. 1520: intercepted commercial messages
subfiles.about: Messages intercepted August 18–27 report trade, shipping and supply negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The traffic concerns rice loading and pricing, silk, rubber, timber, cotton, medicines, textiles and shipping space. Firms discuss import permits, quotas, barter, deteriorating goods and coordination with Japanese authorities across Indochina, China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1798 requesting an assessment of intercepts
subfiles.about: The Embassy asks whether the intercepts warrant continued compilation and forwarding.
subfiles.summary: Gauss requests a decision on the value of despatches 1496 and 1520.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Coordinated Plan of Economic Action in Relation to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a two-volume Export Control planning paper filed elsewhere.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to an economic action plan concerning Japan.

subfiles.title: War Department assessment of commercial intercepts
subfiles.from: Edward H. Miller, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: Military Intelligence states that continued compilation and forwarding is unnecessary for its purposes.
subfiles.summary: Miller reports that Military Intelligence does not need further compilations of the intercepted messages.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1576: Japanese commercial messages
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards messages intercepted August 28–September 11, 1943.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson submits the next group of translated commercial intercepts.

subfiles.title: Enclosure to despatch No. 1576: intercepted commercial messages
subfiles.about: Messages intercepted August 28–September 11 describe commodity trade and wartime transport.
subfiles.summary: The messages range across rubber, rice, rice bags, bran, textiles, machinery, medicines, timber, sugar and industrial chemicals. Several detailed exchanges concern rice losses, warehouse handling, mill equipment and disputes over import control. Other traffic addresses permits, shipping capacity, factory construction and local production.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1609: Japanese commercial messages
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards messages intercepted September 13–16, 1943.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson submits further translated Japanese commercial messages.

subfiles.title: Enclosure to despatch No. 1609: intercepted commercial messages
subfiles.about: Messages intercepted September 13–16 concern mineral surveys, trade and industrial supplies.
subfiles.summary: Traffic covers copper ore investigations, sugar, motorcar parts, cotton cultivation, rice conversion rates, caustic soda, cableways, lumber, shipping craft, ammonia and currency exchange. Several firms seek military certificates, permits and transport space.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1635: Oil production in the N.E.I. and North Borneo
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: The Embassy transmits Dutch reports on oil facility demolition and assesses Japanese restoration.
subfiles.summary: Gauss forwards two Dutch demolition reports and describes a 1942 observation of severe damage at Balikpapan. Dutch Ambassador Lovink believes Japanese oil production has risen since April 1943 but remains below half of prewar output. The Embassy is still seeking information on Japanese production elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Demolition of Royal Dutch Shell oilfields and refineries in the N.E.I.
subfiles.from: Royal Dutch Shell Group report, London
subfiles.about: The report describes planned destruction of oil wells, refineries and equipment before Japanese occupation.
subfiles.summary: Prepared demolition plans were carried out at Balikpapan, Pangkalan Brandan, Pladjoe, Tjepoe/Wonokromo, Tarakan, Boela and New Guinea. The report details cemented and junked wells, destroyed refinery plants, pipelines, stores and records. It estimates that some 3,000 wells were made unusable.

subfiles.title: Report on demolition of Talang Djimar field, 1942
subfiles.about: The report records the destruction of wells and equipment in the Talang Djimar field.
subfiles.summary: Thornton reports that 89 of 92 wells were definitely destroyed, mostly by cementing and dropping tubing and scrap into them. Pumps, boilers, drilling equipment, pipeline facilities and records were also destroyed.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1644: Japanese commercial messages
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards messages intercepted September 20, 22 and 25, 1943.
subfiles.summary: Gauss submits another enclosure of translated commercial intercepts.

subfiles.title: Enclosure to despatch No. 1644: intercepted commercial messages
subfiles.about: The visible messages discuss cotton and hemp cultivation, commodity quotas, kapok and rice bags.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure begins with September 20 traffic on experimental cotton planting, hemp bag manufacture, blankets, milk, kapok shipments and rice bag repairs. September 22 traffic starts with a proposed hemp planting program; the enclosure continues beyond page 281.
